description: We are a team of computer science students from Egypt building Mars Crew: a browser game where kids aged 7 to 12 run a Mars base together and learn the real trade-offs of a space mission, using real NASA data such as DONKI solar flares. We love games, space and making science fun.
summary:
Mars Crew is a free browser game for children aged 7 to 12, in Arabic and English. One to four players run a small base on Mars, in Gale Crater, where NASA's Curiosity rover measures radiation. Each player has one job: the Engineer keeps the power on, the Farmer grows food and fresh air, the Doctor protects the crew from radiation, and Mission Control on Earth watches the Sun. Robots fill any empty job.

There is never enough power, so every choice costs something and the players have to talk it through. The solar storms in the game really happened: they come from NASA's DONKI records with their real dates, and the radio delay between Earth and Mars is worked out for the real date, so a warning from Earth can arrive up to 20 minutes late. Dusty, a friendly robot who speaks in a recorded Egyptian Arabic voice and in English, guides the crew. Every job is a short mini-game that teaches one real fact, and a Science Lab, a Mars Academy, a Mars Explorer with real craters and real rover landings, and two missions based on real NASA events turn NASA's data into things children can try for themselves.
details:
The problem

Children aged 7 to 12 love space, but what they meet is usually facts and posters. They see how missions end, not the decisions that make them work. On Mars every decision has a cost: the air is thin, dust storms cover the solar panels, solar storms bring radiation, and a message from Earth can take up to about 22 minutes to arrive. The challenge asked for a game where children run a Martian or lunar outpost and feel these trade-offs for themselves, using real NASA data instead of invented numbers.

Our solution

Mars Crew turns each part of a real mission into a job for one player, so the trade-offs become real conversations between children. Whatever power one player gets, another player loses. A mission lasts about 15 minutes, every day ends with a short report that links each choice to its result, and losing is safe: the crew can replay the same morning with a new plan.

Every objective of the challenge, in the game

  • Run a Martian outpost: a base in Gale Crater with a greenhouse, labs, a radiation shelter, a sleep room and solar panels outside. A mission lasts 5, 6 or 7 days.
  • Power budgeting: every morning the crew shares a few power bolts between the air machine, plant lights, the storm walls and the radio, and must keep 3 for the night heaters. Dust on the panels lowers tomorrow's power.
  • Life support: Air + Food runs down every day. Suit air runs out outside, so players must go back in to refill. An air leak drains the base until someone patches it.
  • Food production: the Farmer plants, waters and harvests. Plants need light and water and pay back days later, so today's choice decides next week's food and air.
  • Radiation shielding: real solar flares trigger storms. The crew runs to a shelter whose walls hold water; radiation shortens each health bar for the rest of the mission and never heals.
  • Communication delay: Mission Control sees flares first, but warnings reach Mars only after the real light-travel delay for that date (19.8 minutes in February 2026). Earth sees a Mars camera that is minutes old.
  • Real trade-offs: 8 crew dilemmas, a shared power plan, and choices whose results show up days later. Turning the radio off saves power but blocks storm warnings.
  • Real NASA data: 165 real flares from NASA DONKI with their dates and IDs, real photos of the Sun on each flare day from NASA's SDO, Mars terrain from NASA MOLA, a globe from the Viking mosaic, real craters and real landing sites.
  • Ages 7 to 12: short sentences, a robot guide, mini-games instead of menus, "Help me choose" for younger players, and a visible arrow to the next job.
  • Teamwork: 1 to 4 players with split screen. If a teammate goes down, someone has 28 seconds to reach them. Every night the whole crew must meet in the sleep room.
  • Learning that sticks: mini-games that each teach one fact, 11 hands-on experiments, 12 Academy levels with a science question each, and 24 science cards with their sources.
  • Accessible to everyone: full Arabic and English, free, no install, no account, and it still works from saved data when there is no internet.

How does our solution work

1. Meet Dusty, the crew's robot guide

When the game opens, Dusty leaves his corner, grows as he flies to the middle of the screen, and welcomes the player in his own voice, then laughs, winks and returns to his corner. He stays with the crew on every screen: he explains things in short sentences, points to the next job, reacts to what happens with 15 expressions, and has a "Tell me more" button for extra detail.

2. Choose your crew

Each player picks one job and types a name and a suit colour. The four astronauts are drawn in code, with four views and ten expressions each, and their faces and poses follow what is really happening to them.

3. Build the mission (Mission Blueprint)

Before launch, the crew can choose a landing site (Gale, Jezero or Elysium) and up to three instruments inspired by real NASA ones (MEDA weather, RAD radiation, MOXIE oxygen), inside a small budget. The choices change the starting battery, shelter or Air + Food. The game says clearly that these budgets and bonuses are game rules, not spacecraft specifications.

4. A day on Mars

  1. Choose. Every second day the crew votes on a dilemma. Both options cost something.
  2. Share the power. Give power bolts to four machines and keep 3 for the night.
  3. Work. Each player has a sticky-note job list: jobs come in order, and emergencies such as a leak or a hurt teammate jump to the top. Every job is a mini-game.
  4. Survive. Suit air, nightfall, space rocks, dust devils, air leaks and solar storms.
  5. Sleep and learn. At night the whole crew must gather in the sleep room. The night report shows the day's numbers, a real fact about sleep in space, and a new science card.

5. A real solar storm, and a delayed warning

Each mission uses a window of real days from one of four saved periods of NASA DONKI flare records (165 flares, 2016 to 2026). On the hardest level, the Sun is the real February 2026 Sun, with an X8.1 flare on 1 February. Mission Control sees the flare first, but the warning reaches Mars only after the real radio delay for that date. The crew runs to the shelter. After the storm, a "This really happened!" card shows the real Sun on that day, photographed by NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory, with a ring on the flare and its DONKI record.

6. Every job is a mini-game

Each mini-game teaches one idea: wipe the dust off a panel (dust blocks sunlight), find the flare on the Sun and see its class (flares are graded A, B, C, M, X), drill through sand and rock to ice (water on Mars is underground), press repair steps in order (crews follow procedures), keep the dish pointed at Earth, patch a leak before the air escapes, breathe slowly to rest, and more: 15 jobs in total.

7. Mars Academy (solo levels)

One player learns one job at a time: 12 levels, 3 for each job. Each level opens with a hands-on experiment, gives one short job with a goal list, and ends with a science question. Players earn up to 3 stars and become an Expert when they finish a job's path. Example: "Storm warning!" is built on a real X1.5 flare from 3 February 2026.

8. Science Lab

The Science Lab on the main menu holds 11 hands-on experiments: dust on a solar panel, power at night, a water wall against radiation, the health bar, plants and light, ice under the ground, the radio delay, a twin rover on Earth, space rocks, dust storms and the space suit. Each one opens with Dusty's explanation, which he can read aloud in his recorded voice, and a slider or button to try it. Example: in "Power comes from the Sun", the child moves the dust slider and watches the power bolts drop as the panel gets dusty. The lab also holds the sticker album of 24 science cards, each with its fact and its source, and real NASA photos of Mars.

9. Mars Explorer: real places, real craters, real landings

A rotating globe made from the NASA/USGS Viking colour mosaic shows 8 real landing places and 11 named features (10 craters and the Hellas basin). Clicking a crater flies down to a close-up map made from NASA MOLA elevation data, with verified facts, a NASA image with its credit, and Dusty's explanation. From a landing place, children can help one of 9 real spacecraft land the way it really did: parachute, legs, airbags or sky crane. For example, they help Perseverance land in Jezero Crater.

10. Real NASA Event Missions

The Mission Archive holds two short missions based on real events: "The Radiation Surge" (Curiosity's RAD instrument measured its largest radiation surge since landing, on 20 May 2024) and "The Darkened Sky" (the 2018 planet-encircling dust storm tracked by MRO's Mars Climate Sounder). Each has NASA images, an evidence briefing and source links. The debrief keeps "What NASA observed" separate from "What happened in your simulation", so children see the difference between real measurements and the game.

11. Winning and losing

A win is a party with confetti and the whole crew dancing. After a loss, Dusty gives a tip and the crew can go back to the morning of the same day and try a new plan. Between days the crew builds one thing for the base, such as an extra solar panel or a water tank, and it appears on the map.

Dusty's voice and the voice-over

  • Real recorded voice: Dusty speaks Egyptian Arabic with 140 recorded lines, and English with 34 lines. Every clip is a local file; nothing is generated while you play, and no online speech service is used.
  • Lips that follow the voice: the game reads the loudness of each recording every 20 milliseconds, so Dusty's mouth opens on the real syllables and closes in the pauses, in both languages.
  • Always readable: every line is also shown as text in Dusty's speech bubble. The 164 lines that have no recording yet show their text only, and the game never plays a wrong clip in their place.
  • Voice controls: voice on or off, replay, stop and volume, on every screen.
  • The pitch video: Dusty narrates the 30-second video with his real recorded lines, from "Whoever's closest, get there now!" to "Every step helps the crew." Each subtitle shows a small talking Dusty and his name; Arabic lines show the Arabic words with the English translation underneath.

What is real, and what is a game rule

  • Real: every flare's class, date and DONKI ID; the radio delay for the mission date (from JPL planet positions: 11.3 minutes on Perseverance's landing day, NASA's press kit says about 11.4); every science card fact and quiz answer, with its source; crater names, terrain and landing sites.
  • Game rules: a day lasts about 2 minutes and 1 minute of delay is 1 second or less; radiation and health are points out of 100, not millisieverts, and whether a flare reaches Mars is a dice roll by its class; power, Air + Food and water are simple numbers, not engineering values.

Benefits

  • For children: they learn by deciding, not by memorising. Failing is safe, and each report explains what to try next.
  • For teachers and parents: a 15-minute mission, Class mode with discussion questions at big moments, free, nothing to install.
  • For the Arab world: full Arabic, with Dusty speaking Egyptian Arabic, so children can learn space science in their own language.
  • For trust in science: every real number has a source, and the game always says what is a game rule.

Our goal, and our limits

Our goal is to turn NASA's open data into decisions children can make with their friends, so that they understand why a Mars mission is hard, not only that it is. Our limits today: the game has not been playtested with children yet; it is made for PC (keyboard, mouse and gamepad), not phones; 164 of Dusty's lines are still waiting for recordings; and the live NASA flare feed uses NASA's public demo key, which has a low hourly limit, so the game falls back to NOAA and then to its saved NASA records.

Tools and technologies used

  • Game: HTML5 Canvas and plain JavaScript, no game engine and no framework. All game art, sound effects and music are made in code.
  • Data: NASA DONKI flare records, NASA SDO images (through Helioviewer.org), NASA MOLA elevation, the NASA/USGS Viking colour mosaic, the IAU planetary names gazetteer, JPL planet positions, NASA OSDR studies.
  • Testing: Node.js: 89 automated checks (both languages, every source, every mini-game can be finished, survival rules, robot teammates, every file the game loads) and autopilot missions that check that strategy matters.
  • Video: our own tools record the real game in a headless browser and edit the video in code, with music made in code.
  • Hosting: GitHub and Vercel, as a static website. Source code: https://github.com/mohamed-saied-1/mars-crew

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) tools

We used SI tools to help us build the project, while we were brainstorming for creative ideas about the challenge:

  • Coding help: SI coding assistant (Claude) helped us as a helper in test and fix code, check our NASA data against its sources
  • Subtitles: an offline speech-recognition model (Whisper) helped us find the exact words and timing in Dusty's Arabic recordings for the video subtitles.
  • Dusty's Arabic voice is a human recording. The game's art is drawn in code, and the NASA images are real photos shown with their credits. No SI-generated image is presented as NASA data, and no NASA logo or branding is used.
